Opening meats and cheeses
Provolone, Swiss
Cut in half. A small cut along the length, then peel the wrap away.
Boiled ham, cappacuolo, salami, pepperoni
Cut each in half. A small cut along the length, then peel the outside wrap. Cappacuolo, salami and pepperoni have a second wrapping to take off too.
Prosciuttini
Cut the wrapper at the top or the side and take it off. Don't cut it in half.
Turkey
Cut an X on the bottom, not too deep. Peel away both layers of wrap.
Rinse and pat dry
Under cold water, then a paper towel: boiled ham, prosciuttini, cappacuolo, turkey, roast beef, pastrami.
  • Opened meats and cheeses get used within 24 hours.
  • Not rewrapped: into the meat case, FIFO. Rewrapped in plastic after leaving its original package: date it.
  • Ask the manager how much of each to open.

The Production Pro chart

Prep today for what you need today. The chart shows what the store really uses, and in the video's words, "food cost is food used."

  • Count smarter: onions each, lettuce by the pan, tomatoes by the row, bacon by the sheet. One row of 7 tomatoes covers 10.5 loaves.
  • Check the subs against the bread. One pan of lettuce is 4 heads, enough for 20 loaves. If the store used 140 loaves, that should be 7 pans. If 10 went out, 3 pans are going somewhere: too much on each sub, or too much wasted in the trough.
  • Watch what's left. Two pans of lettuce left over every night means it's over-prepped, and day-old lettuce is going on tomorrow's subs.
  • Keep the drop-ins looking full by stepping down to smaller pans through the day.
  • Bread and onions left at night go to the grill the next day and have to be used by 2 p.m. After that they're thrown out.
  • Product mix is how many of each kind of sub the store sells. A store selling 80% cold subs uses more lettuce than one selling half and half.
  • Weather counts. Same forecast as last Monday, about the same prep. Cold and rainy, probably less.

Bread Pan it tonight, proof and bake it in the morning.

Bread 1: panning

The video's line for all three bread lessons: bread is the foundation of every sub. Here is the whole bread day, then the first step.

Panning

  • A clean bread pan and form, the form laid right on the pan.
  • 2 oz of cornmeal, sprinkled evenly in the channels of the form. Too much builds up and blocks the heat from below, so the bread won't bake right. Too little and the bread burns.
  • Frozen loaves into the channels, rib side down. Minis the same way.
  • Slide the pan carefully into the bread rack. When you're done, zip the rack cover closed. It keeps the moisture on the dough while it thaws.
  • Leftover frozen dough: close the bag in the box and get it back in the freezer right away.
  • Roll the rack into the walk-in slowly, so the dough doesn't roll in the channels.
  • Pan after 7 p.m., so the bread thaws properly overnight. Check the amount with the manager or shift leader.
  • Work fast. Frozen dough thaws quickly.

Put the bread day in order

Tap the steps in order.

Bread 2: proofing

Proofing wakes up the yeast, so the dough rises fast.

  • Preheat both. Oven to 350°F. Proofer to 100°F at 85 to 95% relative humidity, usually a setting of 4 to 5. The hygrometer at the bottom of the proofer shows the real number.
  • A warmed-up proofer has a mist on the door, not water running down the glass.
  • Rack out of the cooler: straighten the loaves in the forms, and stretch any short ones to the length of the form.
  • First 5 trays into the top 5 rungs, timer for 25 minutes. Then 5 more trays below them, and another 25 minutes.
  • Be quick with the door. Heat and humidity get out every second it's open.
  • Check the dough now and then. It should be slightly tacky. If it looks dry, spray it with room temperature water.
  • 50 to 70 minutes in all. Proofers and the weather vary, which is where the 20 minutes comes from.
  • White and wheat are proofed separately.
  • Done when the loaf just touches the curve of the bread tool: 2 to 2.5 times its original size.

Bread 3: score, bake, cool, stack

A great bake starts with a proper proof. Nothing you do in the oven makes up for a bad one.

  • Score the white loaves, minis too, with the scoring knife: 1/16 inch deep, down the center, stopping 1.5 inches from each end. Wheat is not scored.
  • Into the oven, door closed right away. Bake 14 to 16 minutes. Wheat may take 1 to 2 minutes longer.
  • Keep the rotation going: when the top 5 rungs of the proofer empty, move the bottom 5 trays up and load 5 more below.
  • At the timer, check the color against the bread color chart on the proofer door: golden brown. Take it out the moment it gets there.
  • Cool on the bottom rungs of the bread rack. Heat rises, so the coolest bread is always on the bottom. The cover stays open while it cools; zip it only when every loaf on the rack is cool.
  • Stack only when it's completely cool. Rub the bottoms of 2 loaves together to knock off the extra cornmeal. Pyramid no more than 3 rows high, 18 to 24 loaves a pan, on the front line bread rack, covered.
  • Busy: a smaller pyramid can sit on the front counter by the slicer. Slow: keep the bread covered and sealed, or the air crusts it.

Floor thaw: bread in a pinch

Short on thawed dough? Frozen loaves can thaw at room temperature in about an hour and a half. It works. Overnight in the cooler is still better.

  • When: a busier day than planned, or anything else that leaves you short.
  • How: let the frozen dough sit in the bread rack at room temperature for an hour and a half, or until it's thawed all the way.
  • Check it often. If it looks dry, mist it with water.
  • Then proof and bake as usual.
  • What you give up: the dough misses its overnight aging, so the color, texture and flavor can come out slightly different. It's still very good bread.
  • The real fix: bake enough in the first place. Track your bread and tell the team, so tomorrow's number is right.

Rosemary parm bread

Bread with Parmesan and rosemary baked on top. Score, mist, cheese, rosemary, bake.

For each loaf

  • Parmesan: half an ounce. About a third of a 4 oz soufflé cup.
  • Rosemary: 1/16 of an ounce. About 2 small pinches.

How

  1. Proof the bread all the way, then score it the way you always do.
  2. Mist it with water. The water is what makes the toppings stick.
  3. Sprinkle the Parmesan across the loaf. Cover the ends.
  4. Rosemary on top of the cheese, so there's rosemary in every bite.
  5. Bake as normal. Make mini loaves the same way.

Good to know

  • Post the rosemary parm chart in the prep area so everyone can see how it's made.
  • Shredded, not grated. Shredded melts nicely.
  • Parmesan: 90-day shelf life, 4 five-pound bags to a case. Extra bags can go in the freezer. An open bag goes into a 4-quart Cambro (a clear food storage tub) in the walk-in.
  • Chopped rosemary: 1,095-day shelf life. That's three years.
  • Show it off in a rush: in front of the slicer, or a few loaves on top of the meat case.
  • Leftover loaves can be stored and used for hot subs the next day.
  • About 20% of your bread is usually rosemary parm. Track it on the production report so you never run out.

Put it in order

Tap the steps in order.

Gluten-free bread

One rule runs the whole thing: nothing that touched regular bread touches this sub. Clean first, fresh gloves, its own paper, its own knife.

The rolls

  • They come fully baked, each one wrapped, 12 to a case.
  • Into the freezer on delivery. Good for up to 6 months frozen.
  • To thaw: pull what you need onto the back counter. Never the bread rack. Leave each roll in its wrapper until it's served.
  • About 40 minutes to thaw, so pull them at 9:15 a.m. as part of opening.
  • Thawed and still wrapped: good for 5 to 7 days. Opened: wrap what's left in plastic right away and use it that day.

A cold sub

  1. Clean the slicer and the counters.
  2. Everyone who will touch the sub washes their hands and puts on fresh gloves.
  3. Tear a sheet of parchment paper. The sub is made on it, start to finish.
  4. Unwrap the roll. Cut it with the clean knife that is only for gluten-free. The lid stays on the paper.
  5. Slice it. The roll is a little smaller, but the meat and cheese portions are the same as a regular or a giant.
  6. Pass the paper, the sub and the knife to the sprinkler, who sprinkles it right on the paper.
  7. Wrap it on a fresh sheet, cutting it with the same gluten-free knife.
  8. Label it GF.
  • All the toppings are gluten-free. For mayo or cherry pepper relish, use the squeeze bottles in the meat case, not the spatulas.

A hot sub

  • Same rules. Clean the grill top, the counters and the tools. Wash hands, fresh gloves, its own parchment, the gluten-free knife.
  • No pocket. Cut the roll all the way through, like a cold sub.
  • Once the fillings are on the bottom half, cut regulars in half and giants in quarters.

Guests who order gluten-free watch every step. Smile, be professional, and do every step every time.

Put it in order

Tap the steps in order.

The grill Hot subs, start to finish, plus bacon and steaks.

Grill basics and hot sub bread
  • Fast, calm, organized. Keep the tickets in the order they came in, and don't start a hot sub until you can give it your attention.
  • Scrape the grill as often as you can. A clean grill cooks quicker.

The bread is a pocket

  • Giants: run the knife across the front of the loaf, angled into the bread. Don't slice through the ends, and don't cut all the way through.
  • Regulars: cut the loaf in half first, then make the same cut in each half.
  • Pre-cut before the rush. It saves time while you're grilling.

Temper it: warm, not toasted

  • Open and close the pre-cut loaf, so the heat can reach the middle without toasting it.
  • Bottom side down on the grill, and turn it often so it warms evenly.
  • Leave it on as long as you can. Take it off when it needs its sauce or toppings.

Cheesesteaks: 17, 43, 56

All three are built on the regular #17. Learn that one and the other two are small changes.

  1. 1

    Bread on the grill to temper. The pre-cut loaf goes on the grill bottom side down, to warm it, not toast it. Open and close it first so the heat can reach the middle. Keep turning it through the whole cook, and leave it on as long as you can.

  2. 2

    Paper torn, cheese laid out. Tear the paper: 15 inches for a regular. Lay out the cheese: 3 slices. A Big Kahuna gets 4.

  3. 3

    Onions down, as long as the bread. Using the length of the bread on the grill as your guide, spread out 1.25 ounces of onions.

  4. 4

    Peppers on top of the onions. Spread 0.75 ounces of peppers to the same length, on top of the onions. The peppers help cook and marinate the onions.

  5. 5

    Steak on, flipped, lightly salted. Place the steak on the grill with the red-handled tongs, and avoid touching the raw meat. Once it's on, flip it and lightly salt it. A good moment to turn the bread.

  6. 6

    Break 4, bring together, break 4. With the red spatula and the red dough cutter, break the steak 4 times. Bring it together and break it 4 more.

  7. 7

    Onions and peppers on top, break 8 more. Put the peppers and onions on top of the steak and break it 8 more times, the same 4 and 4 as before. That's 16 in all.

  8. 8

    Cheese on top, a few slits. Lay the slices of cheese on top of the steak to melt, and cut a few slits in the cheese so it melts faster. Don't overcook the steak while you wait for it.

  9. 9

    Onto the bread, loose bits scraped on. Use the dough cutter to get all of the steak onto the spatula, and place it onto the bread. Scrape the loose bits off the grill and onto the sub.

The break count

The other two

  • #43 Chipotle: once the cheese is laid out, take the bread off the grill, put 3 lines of chipotle mayo on the inside of the lid, and set the bread aside. Then cook it exactly like a 17.
  • #56 Big Kahuna: 4 slices of cheese instead of 3, plus mushrooms and jalapeños. The video gives those amounts on the chicken Kahuna: 0.75 oz of mushrooms and 4 to 5 jalapeños, down with the onions and peppers.
  • Giants: double every portion, and 21 inches of paper. Still cook it as two regular portions, so it goes onto the bread evenly.

Put the #17 in order

Tap the steps in order.

Chicken cheesesteaks: 16, 42, 55

The same build as the beef, with chicken in place of steak.

  • The chicken goes on frozen, so it usually takes a little longer than the thawed beef.
  • Cook it all the way through, and don't dry it out. Move with urgency so it isn't overcooked.
  • Yellow tools: yellow-handled tongs, yellow spatula, yellow dough cutter. Avoid touching the raw meat.
  • Same portions as the 17: 15 inches of paper, 3 slices of cheese, 1.25 oz of onions, 0.75 oz of peppers on top of them.
  • Same breaks: flip, break 4, bring it together, break 4, onions and peppers on top, 8 more. Cheese on top with a few slits. Onto the bread, loose bits scraped on.
  • #42 Chipotle Chicken: 3 lines of chipotle mayo on the inside of the lid, like the 43.
  • #55 Big Kahuna Chicken: 4 slices of cheese, and 0.75 oz of mushrooms and 4 to 5 jalapeños go down with the onions and peppers.
  • Giants: double the portions, 21 inches of paper, cooked as two regular portions.

The video salts the steak right after the flip. For the chicken it only says to flip it.

Chicken with lettuce and tomato: 31, 26, 44

No onions or peppers on these. What changes is what goes on the bread, and when: the lid gets dressed first, and lettuce goes on last.

26 Chicken Bacon Ranch
Lid first: 3 lines of ranch, then bacon, then tomatoes. Grill: chicken, then cheese. Finish: lettuce.
44 Buffalo Chicken
Lid first: 3 lines of blue cheese dressing, then tomatoes. Grill: chicken, then 3 full rows of Frank's RedHot, then cheese. Finish: lettuce.
31 California, not on your board
Lid first: mayo spread in an even layer, then tomatoes. Grill: chicken, then cheese. Finish: lettuce.
How muchRegularGiant
Cheese slices36
Tomato slices35
Bacon slices (the 26)24
Chicken1 piece2 pieces
Lettuce (soufflé cups)24
  • The chicken: flip, break 4, bring it together, break 4, then mix and break 8 more. 16 in all, cooked through without drying it out.
  • Onto the bread evenly, loose bits scraped on. Then the lettuce.
  • Hot subs get less lettuce than cold ones: 2 cups on a regular and 4 on a giant, where a cold sub gets 3 and 5.
  • Lose track of which is which? The hot subs chart is posted for exactly that.

Wrapping hot subs
  • Every grilled sub goes in the hot sub wrap. It holds the heat and lets the sub breathe, so it doesn't go soggy.
  • 15 inches for a regular, 21 for a giant.
  • Giants get cut in half. Regulars don't get cut. That's different from a cold sub.
  • Stand the sub up on its side, so everything stays in place.
  • Wrap it loosely, with the same steps as a cold sub. Never squeeze a hot sub.

Bacon
  • Before you start: grill preheated to 350°F, a 2.5-inch half pan with a grate, the bacon thawed, the steam table preheated.
  • About 4 sheets of bacon on the grill top.
  • Leave it alone. Flipped too early or too often, it sticks and shrivels. It cooks itself loose from the grill, and by then it's about 75% done.
  • Flip several pieces at a time with a spatula, keeping them straight, and cook the last 25% to golden brown.
  • Off the grill several pieces at a time, into the pan, and the pan goes into the steam table.
  • End of the night: leftover bacon can be wrapped and reheated the next day. FIFO.

Steaks: thaw the beef, keep the chicken frozen
  • Both arrive frozen and are stored in the freezer at 0°F.
  • Raw meat: if you touch it, wash your hands and change your gloves before you touch any other food.
  • Beef is panned between 2 and 4 p.m. the day before. The Production Pro chart and the register's production report tell you how much.
  • A 6-inch deep half pan with a drain grate. Stand the frozen steaks up, closed side of the paper facing out, and put the pan in the walk-in.
  • Ready at about 40°F: holding its shape, some ice crystals, still slightly frozen. An overthawed steak goes soft, cooks too fast and can overcook.
  • Chicken stays frozen. The grill person pulls it from the freezer as needed. If the store is busy enough, 4 to 6 frozen chicken steaks at a time can sit in the sandwich unit.
  • Chicken left in the sandwich unit at close is thrown out. It can't be refrozen.

The slicer Cutting bread, slicing in order, and keeping the machine clean.

Slicing: speed starts before the rush

The video's order of things: safe, accurate, friendly, then fast. "Speed is a mentality."

  • Know the menu cold. When a guest says "13," you can't hesitate: every ingredient, in order. That's what the Drill tab is for.
  • Pre-cut a few loaves before the rush, regulars and giants, and restock in the lulls, so bread is grab and go.
  • Ask fewer questions. Don't ask which bread: slice it on white, and the guest will say if they want something else. Don't ask if they want peppers and onions on a hot sub: they'll tell you if they want it changed.
  • More than one at a time. Once the basics are in your hands, take more than one order and slice more than one sub at once.

Cutting bread for cold subs

A good cut gives a sub balanced between its top and bottom, and keeps your fingers out of the way.

  1. Free hand flat on top of the loaf, thumb and pinky lifted. Rest your palm with just enough pressure to hold the bread still. Giants and minis are cut this way as they are.
  2. Start at the butt of the bread: the round end, at the end closest to the guest.
  3. Saw, with the knife level, so the bread comes out in equal halves. Dragging the knuckles of your knife hand along the counter keeps the cut even.
  4. Saw all the way through the far end.
  5. Pass the lid to the sprinkler, set down as close to the sprinkling board as you can, and say which sub is coming and who it's for.

Regulars: cut a giant into two equal halves, point the round ends toward the guest, then cut each one the same way.

Stance, push, catch, flip
  • Athletic stance: feet about shoulder width apart and parallel, a little bend in the knees. Staggered feet make you lean into the slicer, your back pays for it, and someone walking behind you can trip on your foot.
  • A small step back from the slicer. Too close and you rock back and forth and bump into it.
  • Elbow down. With your elbow up, your shoulder and head drop and you lose the guest. Elbow down: shoulders back, head up, standing straight.
  • Let the slicer do the work. The blade is sharp. Push straight through; don't press down into it.

Push only the length of the product. Going end to end on every stroke is wasted motion.

  • The hands work together. Every time the right hand pushes forward, the left comes in under the blade to catch. As the left flips the slice onto the sub, the right is already coming back.
  • The right hand never stops. Stopping it while you flip is what breaks the rhythm.
  • Eyes: on the sub while you learn, since the meat comes out in the same spot every time. Then up, on the guest.

Meat case, guard, hands
  • Few steps to the meat case and back, and close the meat case door every time you take something out.
  • Place product in gently. Dropping or tossing it in wears the slicer out.
  • "Bring the guard to the party." The guard goes on top of the product every time. It holds the product in place and keeps you off the blade.
  • As the guard comes down, the left hand sets the dial. Setting it turns the slicer on.
  • Right thumb locked in behind the pusher deck, fingers resting on the guard. Not on the handle: the handle pulls your elbow up. A little pressure from your fingers gives a slightly thicker slice when you need one.
  • Taking product out: guard off, right hand slides the product into your left, back to the meat case, door closed. Never reach in with your left hand.

Setting the thickness, every day

Thickness changes the flavor and the value. Too thick: the flavor is off, the meat is hard to flower, and it costs the store. Too thin: there isn't enough meat on the sub, and the guest may not come back.

  • The scale first: power on, a sheet of paper down, then tare so the paper doesn't count.
  • Cheese (provolone and Swiss) is set with provolone: 5 slices should weigh 2 oz.
  • Meat is set with boiled ham: 8 slices should weigh 4.75 oz.
  • Heavy or light? Move the dial and slice again until it lands.
  • Every morning. The test slices get used: provolone goes to the grill for hot subs, ham goes on call-in orders or employee meals.

Slicing the sub

The transcript of the video spells it "flour." The move is flowering: the slice gathers on your fingertips instead of lying flat.

  • The slice guide is a guide, not a rule. It lists the slices for each sub. If a slice comes out as half a slice, add another.
  • Equal distribution. Every meat covers the sub end to end: the end nearest the guest and the end nearest you. Every bite has every product.
  • Proper sequence. Slice in the order the slice guide lists them.
  • One-meat subs go on in layers. The #7 gets about 10 slices of turkey, in 2 layers of about 5.
  • No double pumping: pushing through twice and catching once. It takes height off the sub, and height is the value the guest sees.

Weighing subs

Two reasons: the guest gets what they paid for, and the store doesn't give its food cost away.

  • Tell the guest what you're doing. Say you're putting their sub on the scale to check yourself and make sure they get enough meat and cheese. Without that, it looks like skimping.
  • Never take slices off. If anything, add one or two.
  • Weigh as many online, call-in and catering orders as you can.
  • Pick one sub a day (say the #8) and weigh as many of those as you can.
  • At least 3 subs every shift you slice.
  • Memorize the weights, so you aren't looking at the slice guide every time.

Sub in a tub
  1. Deli sheet flat on the counter. A tub always gets the regular-size portion.
  2. Cheese first, laid flat on the sheet.
  3. The flowered meats, flat on the cheese. On a #13: boiled ham, then prosciuttini.
  4. The round meats, diagonally on top. On a #13: cappacuolo, then salami, then pepperoni.
  5. Roll it up, neat and tight.
  6. Cut 5 times: 6 equal pieces.
  7. 2 pinches of lettuce in the tub (2 soufflé cups), and the pieces laid neatly on top.
  8. The sprinkler does it Mike's Way, the same as any regular. Lid closed tight. Fork and knife.

Hot subs: ask if they'd like lettuce on the bottom, then the hot sub mixture goes in the container.

Put the tub in order

Tap the steps in order.

Wiping down the slicer

When: after each order. Before a veggie sub. After any sub with roast beef. In any break in the rush. And always before you walk away.

  1. Turn the dial clockwise until the blade is completely closed. That turns the slicer off.
  2. Loosen the black knob on the side and let the pusher deck swing open. That locks the dial and the blade closed.
  3. The towel: soaked in warm sanitizer solution, wrung out well, folded into 12.

Then wipe, in this order:

Swing the pusher deck back into place and tighten the black knob.

Put the wipe-down in order

Tap the steps in order.

Cleaning the slicer, every 4 hours

Like every food contact surface, the slicer gets fully taken apart, washed, rinsed and sanitized every 4 hours.

Have ready: 2 metal mesh safety gloves, a container of warm soapy water, one of rinse water, one of warm sanitizer solution, and clean towels, with one kept back to dry the slicer. Wash your hands and put on clean gloves first.

  1. Dial clockwise, blade closed, slicer off. Then unplug it.
  2. Black knob loose, pusher deck swung open.
  3. Small black knob on the guard: take off the spike plate. Then take off the blade plate. Carry both to the three-compartment sink to be washed, rinsed and sanitized.
  4. Metal mesh gloves on.
  5. The blade: a soapy towel folded in 12, from the center outward, slowly. The back of the blade the same way.
  6. Thread the towel from the front between the blade and the guard ring, and turn the blade and towel by hand, pressing the towel lightly against the inside of the ring.
  7. The rest, top down: pusher deck from the outside in, adjustable deck front to back, the side, the towel fed through underneath from front to back, then the bay.
  8. Rinse: all the same steps with a towel soaked in rinse water. Sanitize: all the same steps with a towel soaked in warm sanitizer.
  9. Dry it with the clean towel, put it back together, plug it in. Then clean the mesh gloves by their own instructions.

Guests and the line Greeting, the slicer as quarterback, sprinkling three at once, the wrapper's other jobs.

Guests first

Two moments decide what a guest remembers: how they were greeted and how they were thanked. The rest is being yourself and paying attention.

Greet them, in three places

  • Outside: eye contact, a smile, a quick hello. Look for a way to help, like walking a shopping cart back. Pick up any trash you pass.
  • Inside: the same, plus things like opening a door or clearing a table during the rush.
  • At the slicer: greet in the way that fits the person. Recognize your regulars. If someone is new, offer help or a suggestion, and give them room.
  • Be yourself. No scripted "Welcome to Jersey Mike's." They know where they are. Introduce yourself.
  • Learn names. A hot sub ticket has the guest's name on it. Look at their face too, so you know them next time.

While they're here

  • Customers first. When a guest walks in, everyone stops what they're doing and comes to the front line.
  • Banter means friendly small talk. The training calls it "share your life." It has to be natural, and respectful.
  • Keep the talk on the guest. No personal conversations with each other in front of them.
  • 360° vision: know what's happening in the whole store, not just at your station.
  • Peripheral hearing: listen to the whole store while you work, and act on what you hear.
  • Say the order to the next station. Never ask a guest what they had.
  • Urgency: fast and accurate, moving with purpose, and safe.

Thank them

A real thank you to every guest, every single time. The least they should leave thinking is: "I'm going back."

The slicer runs the line

The slicer is the quarterback. They set the pace, watch the whole line, and own anything that goes wrong on it.

  • Experience first, speed second. The slicer watches the front of the line more than the back, and makes sure each order was made right.
  • Controls the pace. Full speed when the line can take it. Slower when the sprinkler or wrapper is backing up.
  • No more than 3 subs at a time. It sets the pace, leaves a moment to check on the team, and means fewer mistakes.
  • Says it down the line: what the sub is and who it's for. The sprinkler tells the wrapper, the wrapper tells the cashier. Nobody has to ask the guest again.
  • Head up. You can't see the whole store looking down.
  • Calls an audible when it's needed. That means changing the play: stop slicing to help sprinkle, or move someone to the spot that's behind. Don't let the grill back up. Send the wrapper to help.
  • Aces in their places: at the start of a shift or a rush, your best people are in their best spots.
  • Takes the blame. On the slicer you aren't only running the slicer. You're running the store.
  • Follows the sub down the line. For example, checks that every club got its bacon.

Seconds count

  • Unwrap everything you'll use before the rush.
  • Pre-tear the hot sub tickets and offset them, so they pull apart fast.
  • Slicer close to the meat case (fewer steps) and close to you (less reach).
  • Pass the sub before you put the last meat away.

The goal, as the training puts it: not to make any one sub faster, but to serve more guests in the same amount of time.

Sprinkler: speak Mike's Way

The sprinkler keeps up with the slicer by sprinkling three subs at once. The trick is to turn every order into Mike's Way, plus or minus something.

  • Speed first, experience second. If the slicer passes 3 subs, sprinkle 3 at a time. Build up to it.
  • Convert the order. "Lettuce, tomatoes, vinegar, oil and spices" is Mike's Way, no onions. One thing to remember, not five.
  • Go topping by topping across all three subs. The hints in the picture tell you which sub is different.
  • Say it back. "That's Mike's Way, no onions, plus mayo and banana peppers." Invite them to order it that way next time. It takes a few visits.
  • Explain Mike's Way loud enough that the next guests in line hear it too.
  • The Sprinkle Dance: two sprinklers whenever possible. One does onions and steps around while the other does lettuce, then comes back for tomatoes, and so on, talking the whole time.

Set up for speed

  • 2 sets of bottles and shakers.
  • Backup extras ready, like the pickle bucket already open.
  • 2 squeegees.
  • Vinegar and oil caps clean and tight.

Wrapper: organize, help, expedite

The wrapper is the last person to touch the sub and the first to help everyone else.

  • Speed first, experience second.
  • Organize. Know what every sub is, where it is, and who it's for: front line, digital line, grill, call-ins, catering. Know the names on waiting orders, so pickup is quick.
  • Help the cashier. Ask "chips and a drink?" or "a fresh baked cookie?" yourself. Ask "Are you a Shore Points member?" and point them to enter their phone number at the terminal. Tell the cashier everything you can, so they can ring, smile and give the total.
  • Be the second sprinkler. "Avoid the wrapper lean" means don't stand waiting. Dress the lids with mayo, bacon and cherry pepper relish. Join the Sprinkle Dance. Don't wait to be asked.
  • Expedite. That means getting finished food to the right guest. Every hot sub gets worked into the front line. Use the hot sub ticket to tell the cashier and to find the guest. Don't yell the name. Bring it to them when you can.
  • Last line of defense. Listen as the guest orders, so you know the sub is right. Lift the lid on a club to check for bacon.
  • Never pull a guest ahead in line to ring them up.
  • Spot ways to help: restock the toppings, carry out a big order, check the tables.
  • The last impression is yours: a sincere thank you and a smile.

Pass the check What a trainer watches for at each station, as lists you can tick.

How a check works

Each station is trained in three kinds of shift. Introduction: the trainer shows you. Practice: you do it with them beside you. Confidence: they watch you work a real shift and tick a list.

Miss something and it isn't a fail. They talk it through, show it again, and you practice it. Everything ticked means the manager hears you're confident at that station.

The lists below are those confidence lists, in plain words. Tick the lines you already do without thinking. Your ticks stay on this phone only.

Sprinkler check

What the trainer watches for while you sprinkle.

  • I look up, smile, and talk with the guest and the team.
  • I ask "Mike's Way?"
  • The sub goes all the way down the board. Then it doesn't move.
  • Right amount and technique: onions, lettuce, tomatoes, the juice, the spices, extras.
  • I sweep the board before the juice.
  • Clubs always get their bacon and mayo.
  • Everything is spread evenly, ends covered.
  • Lids go on gently.
  • I pick subs up by the ends. No sliding.
  • My area stays clean and stocked.
  • I move with urgency and stay accurate.

After you pass, keep working on

  • 2 rows of juice for 2 oz, at least 8 times out of 10.
  • The Sprinkle Dance.
  • 3 subs at one time.
  • Running the sprinkling drills with a new person.

Wrapper check

What the trainer watches for while you wrap.

  • Eyes up, smiling, joining the banter.
  • Paper pulled to the right length, one sheet at a time.
  • Sub picked up by the ends and set in the center of the paper.
  • Cut properly: hand cupped, knife kept in a safe place.
  • Proper pullback, then the quarter turn.
  • Ends wrapped tight. No wings sticking out.
  • Hand-over-hand roll. No folds, thumbs stay down.
  • A neat, tight wrap, sub facing the right way.
  • Bag popped and creased properly.
  • I tell the cashier what's coming, and mark the number on the bag.
  • I move with urgency and stay accurate.

The extras a strict eye looks for

  • You ask "For here?" and never "To go?" It's more inviting.
  • You don't ask how many times to cut the sub. Use that moment to talk with the guest.
  • More than 2 items get bagged. A 12 lb. bag holds 3 to 4 subs, a 20 lb. bag 4 to 5. Subs first, then drinks, then chips and cookies.
  • You hand the bag to the guest. You don't slide it across the counter.
  • Digital orders are sealed in handled bags, hot subs on top of cold or packed apart, napkins in, and double-checked.

After you pass, keep working on

  • No wrapper lean.
  • Keeping orders organized, hot subs included.
  • Add-ons, and helping the cashier.
  • Running the wrapping drills with a new person.

Cashier check

What the trainer watches for at the register.

  • Eyes up, smiling, joining the banter.
  • I know the register's functions and parts.
  • I ring sales in correctly.
  • I ring in discounts and coupons.
  • I can handle refunds, voids and cancels.
  • Money habits: no gloves on money, hands washed.
  • I can activate and load gift cards.
  • I can use Shore Points.
  • I can use the Customer Facing Terminal, the screen the guest uses.
  • I know the money handling do's and don'ts.
  • I move with urgency and stay accurate.
  • I thank every guest and mean it.

Cashier training also covers register safety, and spends thirty minutes on the robbery section of the Safety First booklet. Ask your manager to walk you through it.

Grill check

What the trainer watches for at the grill.

  • I talk with guests and the team, and I'm smiling.
  • Bread cut and tempered properly.
  • Vegetables portioned properly.
  • Right order: the steak goes down last.
  • Steak salted after the flip.
  • Right chopping technique and count.
  • Tools held properly.
  • I can make beef, chicken and portabella subs the right way.
  • I know how the cheesesteaks differ.
  • Fillings spread evenly on the sub.
  • Every hot sub in the hot sub paper, wrapped loosely.
  • No more than three subs at a time.
  • Grill scraped between subs as needed.
  • I move with urgency and stay accurate.

The extras a strict eye looks for

  • You never start a sub on a dirty spot. Scrape first.
  • Tools by color: red handles for beef, yellow for chicken, black for mushrooms.
  • No banging the tools.
  • A regular portion of onions (1.25 oz) and peppers (0.75 oz) is on display by the grill, so anyone can check by eye.
  • The finished hot sub and its ticket go to the register together. If you bring it to a guest, find them. Don't shout their name.

After you pass, keep working on

  • Splitting the work when two people are on the grill.
  • Keeping up with tickets without overloading the grill.
  • Running the grill tools drill with a new person: 16 breaks, 4 x 4 x 4 x 4.

Slicer check

What the trainer watches for on the slicer.

  • I greet the guest, start the banter, and smile.
  • I tell the team the sub and who it's for.
  • Safe at every step: posture, loading and unloading, the guard.
  • Bread cut right, lids placed next to the sprinkling board.
  • Catch and flip. Built up, not out. Piled high.
  • Equal distribution, ends covered.
  • Cheese thickness: 5 slices of provolone = 2 oz.
  • Meat thickness: 3 slices of ham = 1.8 oz.
  • Meat case door shut every time.
  • Hot sub tickets written right.
  • Subs passed by the ends.
  • 2 to 3 subs at a time, and the line keeps moving.
  • Eyes up, 360° vision: I watch everything.
  • Slicer wiped often enough. I can clean it, sharpen it, oil it, take it apart and put it back.
  • I move with urgency and stay accurate.

The ham number shows up three ways in the training: 3 slices for 1.8 oz on this list, 5 slices for about 3 oz on the fundamentals sheet, and 8 slices for 4.75 oz in the video. All three are the same thickness, about 0.6 oz a slice.

The extras a strict eye looks for

  • 5 hot, wet towels ready, and the slicer wiped after every order.
  • White bread unless the guest says otherwise. You don't ask "White, wheat or rosemary?"
  • The scale is in place and working. Pens are uncapped and tickets pre-torn on top of the meat case.
  • You weigh subs through the rush, and digital, phone and catering orders regularly. Never take slices off a heavy sub.
  • The bread knife is sharp and kept next to the meat case, blade facing away.

After you pass, keep working on

  • Controlling the pace of the line.
  • Peripheral hearing.
  • Changing the play when it's needed.
  • Taking responsibility.
  • Head up, eye contact, every guest.
2

Shift lead

Run a shift.

Run the shift

Knowing the rule is one thing. Using it while the line is out the door is another. Each of these puts you in a spot, asks for a call, then changes the situation and asks again. Every answer is something the training says outright.

Lead the shift The day by the clock, the mid-day checklist, training someone new.

The day by the clock

A store day has six parts. Each part has its own job, and each one sets up the next.

The times are the training's examples. Your store's hours and rushes may sit a little earlier or later.

About 2 hours before the doors Open
Everything on. Bread proofed and baked in three waves. Cookies. Meatballs and sauce. Onions, lettuce and tomatoes sliced. Bacon. Slicer sharpened, oiled, cleaned, thickness set. Gluten-free rolls out at 9:15. Meat case and tea set. Who: the opener, then a second person. Tool: the opening checklist and the Production Pro chart.
Usually 11 to 2 Lunch rush
No prep. Best people in their best spots. The slicer runs the line, three subs at a time at most. Every sub is called down the line. Slicer wiped after each order. A guest walks in, everyone comes forward.
After lunch Mid-day
The mid-day checklist: temperatures logged, sanitizer changed, everything restocked, a full slicer clean. Bread, bacon and cookies topped up if needed. Yesterday's bread and onions leave the grill at 2. Tomorrow's beef is panned between 2 and 4. Tomorrow's lettuce, onions and tomatoes are prepped. The closing lead asks the day lead how the day went.
Usually 5 to 7 Dinner rush
Same as lunch. Before it starts: any extra prep is done, and the closers have split the closing checklist in a quick huddle.
Evening Close down
Dishes as you go. Restock. Half the meat case wrapped. Walk-in mopped, then bread racked after 7. Grill pre-cleaned with oil and a screen. Slicer cleaned one piece at a time. Guests are served right up to closing time. Never fewer than 2 people in the store.
After the doors lock Reset
Dining room, bathrooms and counter area mopped. Everything back in its place so the opener can grab and go. Production Pro chart finished: waste and left filled in.

Put the day in order

Tap the parts of the day in order.

The mid-day checklist

Between the rushes the store gets put back to full: temperatures logged, sanitizer fresh, everything restocked, tomorrow's prep confirmed.

This follows a mid-day checklist as one store's tablet shows it. Yours may differ a little, and the tablet is the one that counts. Tick these to practice. Your ticks stay on this phone only.

1. Temperatures: read, write down, log

WhereShould read
Walk-in cooler36 to 41°F
Freezer0°F, give or take 10
Grill top surface350°F, give or take 10
Hot subs unit36 to 41°F
Bacon warmer (the bacon itself)115 to 145°F
Meat case: the tuna36 to 41°F
Meat case: the display, thermometer between two display hams36 to 41°F
Second line meat case, if you have one36 to 41°F
Drop-ins (the cold wells that hold the toppings)36 to 41°F

2. Sanitizer

  • Test strip for the sink reads 200 to 500 ppm. Photo taken.
  • Test strip for the bucket reads 200 to 500 ppm. Photo taken.
  • Red sanitizer buckets replaced with fresh sanitizer (every 4 hours).
  • Wash and sanitizer sinks changed.
  • Dishes washed, rinsed, sanitized.

3. Where guests are

  • Tables and chairs cleaned.
  • Dining room floor swept and mopped as needed.
  • Chip racks filled, rotated and dusted.
  • Drink coolers filled and rotated, oldest bottles in front.
  • Soda station checked and stocked. Cups restocked.
  • Syrup boxes and CO2 checked.
  • Napkins restocked, dispensers cleaned.
  • Every trash can checked and emptied.
  • Glass cleaned: sneeze guard, front door, meat case, soda case.
  • Bathrooms cleaned, sanitized and swept.

4. The line and the grill

  • Bread checked, and more baked if needed.
  • Slicer fully cleaned, and written on the slicer cleaning form.
  • Front and back line toppings cleaned and restocked to full.
  • Hot sub area cleaned and restocked.
  • Grill tools (tongs, spatulas) washed and rotated.
  • Front line tools (knives, spatulas) washed and rotated.
  • Ice bath on the digital line changed, if your store has one.
  • Vinegar and oil bottles cleaned and filled.
  • Meat case restocked.
  • Bacon checked, and more cooked if needed.
  • Cookies checked, and more baked if needed.
  • The scale cleaned in detail.
  • Mini cookie dough cut and prepped.
  • Production chart updated for everything above.
  • Front line checked one last time: fully stocked.

The tablet tags the first restock line and this last one "9:59." The training sheets print the same tag next to "clean and restock when there is a break in the action."

5. Tomorrow

  • Lettuce and onions prepped for tomorrow.
  • Tomatoes sorted and washed.
  • Tuna and chicken salad checked.
  • Freezer pulls done: Philly steak and bacon.
  • Kitchen swept and mopped. Freezer floor swept.

The store's list also has cash tasks and ends with the manager's initials. Your manager will show you those in person.

Training someone new

Show it, do it beside them, then watch them do it. Always say why. That's the whole method.

  • Introduction shift: you demonstrate at normal speed, then slowly, explaining the why of each move.
  • Practice shifts: they do it, first away from guests, then side by side with you on the line for 1 to 2 hours. Coach politely. Step in when needed.
  • Confidence shift: you watch them work and tick the list for that station. Anything missed: talk it through, show it, let them practice, and tell the manager.
  • As they get the hang of it, push the speed.
Go to the check lists (level 1)

Station by station

Sprinkling
Onions, lettuce and tomatoes on the prep table, 30 minutes (10 on each). The juice into the sprinkle pan with water, 20 minutes: 2 rows should weigh 2 to 2.2 oz in the giant pan, 1 to 1.1 oz in the regular. Oregano with cornmeal into clean bread forms, 10 minutes. Then the front line.
Wrapping
Show the wrap, 30 minutes. Practice bread is 2 regular loaves stacked, smashed and wrapped in plastic. Then a Round Robin, 15 minutes: they wrap and bag one, hand it to you, you unwrap it and slide it back. Then the front line.
Cashier
The register side by side, 30 minutes: safety, the screens, a card, cash and gift card sale, counting change back, Shore Points, voids, cancels, refunds. Then 30 minutes on the robbery section of the Safety First booklet. Then the front line.
Hot subs
The tools, 10 minutes: onions on the grill, broken 16 times in a 4 x 4 x 4 x 4 pattern. Tickets, 5 minutes: slicer to grill to cashier. The charts, 5 minutes. Then a regular 17, 16 and 26 outside the rush, 30 minutes. Then the grill in a rush, with you beside them.
Slicing
Safety, the wipe-down, the full clean and cutting bread, 30 minutes. Posture and movements without slicing, 30 minutes. Thickness, coverage and weight, 1 hour: 5 slices of provolone for 2 to 2.2 oz, 5 of ham for 3 to 3.2 oz. Building a sub layer by layer on the scale, 30 minutes. First real subs come from digital or catering orders. Then the front line, with you watching everything.

Beyond the station, keep coaching

  • Keeping their area stocked and clean.
  • Checking the dining room.
  • Helping teammates.
  • Coming to the counter every time a guest walks in.
  • Finishing the checklist.

Opening Two hours, in order, with the prep clock and the sharpener.

An opening in 2 hours

An opening fits in 2 hours when jobs overlap. Bread proofs while you slice. Bacon cooks while you slice tomatoes. Move with urgency and tick the checklist.

  1. Turn on all the equipment, so everything is at temperature when you need it.
  2. Music on, low enough to hear the phone and online orders. The TV stays off until right before open.
  3. Wash your hands and put on gloves. Wash often, all morning.
  4. Stretch all the bread. Fill and set up the sinks while you do.
  5. Cookies in. By the time the bread is stretched, the oven is hot.
  6. Check the bread count: what was racked, what was left over. Fill in the Production Pro chart as you go.
  7. Go time. Meatballs and sauce on the grill.
  8. Slice the onions and lettuce. Bring product, pans and lids to the slicer first. Check the chart for how much. Two at a time, one in front of the other. Cut in the lettuce left from yesterday.
  9. Second person arrives. See where you are and tell them what's needed. The register till and cash box get set up now.
  10. Check the meatballs and sauce, and start the bacon. After raw bacon: new gloves, washed hands.
  11. Slice the tomatoes, checking the bacon and the bread as you go.
  12. Set up the meat case and the tea urns. Clean the grill top.
  13. The checklist: confirm nothing was missed, and hand out the 10 to 10:30 tasks.

What makes it work

  • Layering. Start the job that runs by itself (bread, bacon, cookies), then do the hands-on one.
  • Check the bread often the whole time you're slicing.
  • Clean as you go.
  • Slicing on the front counter? Lean a large Cambro lid against the sneeze guard in front of the slicer. Cleanup is easier.
  • Tick the opening checklist as you finish each task, even if you've opened hundreds of times.

The video also says "remember floor time" when the bread comes out. It doesn't say how long. Ask your trainer how long your store rests the dough before it goes in the proofer.

Put the opening in order

Tap the steps in order.

The prep clock, 8 to 10

The training's timing sheet for an opener who starts at 8 and is ready at 10. It shows how long each job should take.

StartsJobTakes
8:05Preheat, stretch the bread, pan the cookiesabout 10 min
8:15Bread, first 5 pans: white, rosemary, minis50 proof, 14 bake
8:1524 cookies13 min
8:3014 sheets of bacon32 min
8:3512 onions7 min
8:40Bread, next 5 pans: wheat, mini wheats50 proof, 14 bake
8:4726 heads of lettuce14 min

9:06120 tomatoes, or 17 rows15 min

  • The sheet asks three things about the opener. Are they fully trained? Do they use the production report and the Production Pro chart? Do they move with urgency? Its words: openings are a sprint.
  • These are the sheet's example amounts. Your chart tells you how much your store needs.

The sheet shows about 5 minutes between the onions, the lettuce and the tomatoes. It doesn't label that gap. A slicer wipe-down between products fits there.

Sharpen and oil the slicer

Every morning, as part of opening: sharpen for 10 seconds, hone for a second and a half, clean off the metal dust, then a few drops of oil.

Why: a sharp, oiled slicer gives the best slice, doesn't shred the meat, and keeps food cost in line.

You need

  • A clean slicer.
  • The sharpener, with clean, dry stones.
  • The slicer's machine oil, or a food-grade lubricating oil.
  • Cut-resistant metal mesh gloves and eye protection. Both are required.

Sharpen

  1. Put on the metal mesh gloves.
  2. Slicer off. Attach the sharpener, set to 0, and tighten its small knob. The blade is opened all the way.
  3. Put on eye protection.
  4. Switch the slicer on. Turn the sharpener's dial to the first setting for 10 seconds.
  5. Dial back to 0. Slicer off. Wait until the blade stops turning.
  6. Switch on again. Second setting for 1.5 seconds. This hones the edge.
  7. Slicer off. Wait for the blade to stop. Take the sharpener off and close the blade right away.
  8. Brush the stones quickly.
  9. Unplug the slicer and do a complete clean. Sharpening leaves metal dust.

Oil

  • A few drops on the shaft underneath. Slide the pusher deck back and forth to spread it.
  • A few drops on the shaft the guard glides on. Work the guard up and down a few times.
  • It doesn't take much.

Looking after the sharpener

  • Dirty stones stop working. The grinding stone should feel slightly rough.
  • It can be washed and sanitized at the 3-compartment sink. Use its brush, or a toothbrush like it, on the stones.
  • Let the stones dry before the next use. Wet stones can't sharpen.

Slicers come with one of two kinds of sharpener, and they attach in different ways. Have a trained person show you yours on the machine. Don't learn that part from a page.

Put it in order

Tap the steps in order.

Closing Start early, reset for tomorrow, lead the team.

Closing faster

A fast close starts hours before the doors lock, and it never costs a guest their sub.

All evening

  • Wash dishes as you go. A few take no time. A pile costs someone 20 minutes at the end of the night.
  • Fill the chip racks and soda case early, then top them off.
  • Change out the pans in the sandwich unit, steam tables and toppings early, and restock before close.
  • An empty sauce bottle gets washed, rinsed and sanitized. Never just refilled.
  • After the case doors are clean, put plastic wrap on the handles so they don't smudge.

Later in the evening

  • Close half the meat case. Wrap the extra meats and cheeses. Keep out the ones you still need.
  • Sweep and mop the walk-in and freezer before the bread is racked, so the racks never have to be moved.
  • Two people rack the bread if you can. It's quicker and the dough doesn't start to defrost.
  • Pre-clean the grill with oil and a grill screen, while it's still on. Wear oven mitts. Don't use a grill brick yet: it leaves a residue you can't clear fast if someone orders a hot sub.
  • Clean the slicer one piece at a time. Take one piece to the sink, wash, rinse, sanitize, put it back. The slicer is never more than one piece from ready.
  • Clean the dining room, bathrooms and counter area. Don't mop them until the store is closed.

The rule over all of it

  • You serve guests right up to closing time. Never turn one away because something has been cleaned.
  • A hot sub on a pre-cleaned grill cooks fast, and a grill is easy to clean again after one or two subs.
  • If the slicer is apart, put it back together quickly and serve them with a smile.

A great close is a great open

Closing means resetting the store. Whatever tonight's team skips, tomorrow's opener has to make up before they can start.

Everything in its place

  • Grill: utensils washed and back at the grill shelf and steam tables.
  • Front counter: knives, bottles, shakers, the sprinkling board and the trough back in place.
  • Tea urns reset, spigots closed.

Product ready to grab and go

  • Onions peeled and washed.
  • Lettuce bopped and washed.
  • Tomatoes red, ripe, rinsed and ready.
  • All of it prepped the day before and waiting in the walk-in. Nothing slows an opening like having to prep these.
  • The extras (pickles, peppers) topped off, so the opener only has to drain and fluff them.

Every area set

Dining room, fountain counter, chip racks, soda case, bathrooms, grill area, front counter, kitchen and sinks.

If you're the opener

  • Something was missed? Say so. Tell the manager and the team. It isn't the end of the world, but they need to know.
  • Then do the same for the next shift. Before you leave, set them up.
  • A bad opening follows the store all day. A surprise catering order or a call-off on top of it turns a normal morning hectic.

Leading the close

You have the keys. Your job is to keep guests first, keep everyone moving through the checklist, and hand tomorrow a clean start.

  1. Ask the daytime shift leader how the day went. You learn if the after-lunch checklist is done, and if you need extra prep.
  2. Do any extra prep before the dinner rush is in full swing: bread, bacon, produce. You don't want to run out.
  3. Check for catering orders for tomorrow. Set up the boxes and do the extra prep. Write that prep on the Production Pro chart.
  4. Huddle. A quick one, to divide the closing checklist. Everyone knows who is doing what.
  5. Start the closing list early. Before the dinner rush is the time for the more thorough cleaning.
  6. Initial each task as it's finished.
  7. Finish the Production Pro chart: fill in waste and left. That gives you usage.

How a good lead acts

  • The customer comes first. When one walks in, everyone stops and serves them. That's a must.
  • Offer help. "Can I help you with that?" Never hesitate to help with someone else's task.
  • Stay active when it's slow. When the rush dies down, rally the team around the checklist.
  • If you start a task, finish the task.
  • Something clean gets dirty again? No big deal. Wipe it. Keeping things clean and stocked all night is what saves time.
3

Manager

Run the store.

Manager words, in plain English

The words the manager videos use, one line each. Come back here whenever a card uses one you don't know.

Food and counting

COGU
Cost of goods used: what the food and paper you used cost. COGS, cost of goods sold, means the same thing.
Beginning, working and closing inventory
The dollar value of the food and paper in the store at the start of the period. That plus what was delivered. And what's left at the end.
Actual food cost
What food cost was for the period.
Theoretical food cost
What it should have been.
Goal
Theoretical plus 2 points.
Variance
The gap between what was used and what should have been. Red, or negative: too much was used. Black, or positive: too little.
Vendor unit
How a product is packed. 4/1 gal is 4 one-gallon bottles to a case.
Inventory unit
How a product is counted: by the pound, case, box, sleeve, each, bag or gallon.
Reconcile
Match a delivery's paper invoice to what's in CrunchTime, until over/short reads 0.
Purchase journal
The CrunchTime report that lists the period's orders and shows which ones are reconciled.
Post
The last click of an inventory. After it, you pull the report.
Production Pro chart
The daily prep sheet. On hand, plus what was prepped, minus waste, minus what's left, equals what was used.

People and hours

Forecast
A reasonable assumption about upcoming sales, made from the numbers you have.
Coverage chart
For each hour of each day: how many fully trained people the store needs.
Labor percent
What the shifts cost, divided by forecasted sales.
Audible
Changing the play mid-shift when the day calls for it.

Money

P&L
Profit and loss statement. The monthly report on the store's financial health.
Top line
The store's total sales.
Bottom line
What's left after the costs.
Gross sales and net sales
Gross is everything produced, before discounts and coupons. Net is the money that actually came in.
EBITDA
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. It's the bottom of the store's P&L.
CAM
Common area maintenance. Part of the rent line: landscaping, snow removal, the roof.
Over and short
The cash that should be in the drawer, compared with what was deposited.
KPI
Key performance indicator. A number on the CrunchTime dashboard that shows how the store is doing.
POS
The register system.

Guests

Four walls marketing
Everything inside the store that makes an impression on a guest.
Grassroots
Going out near the store, saying who you are, and inviting people in to try it.
Bounce back coupon
A card handed over at the register as a surprise, to bring the guest back: free chips and a drink, or $1 off.
Shore Points
The rewards points. The simple way to say it: buy 12 subs, get the 13th free.

Ordering CrunchTime, the order guide, the slash box.

CrunchTime in one minute

CrunchTime is the software that tracks the store's food, orders, counts and labor. In the store you use the part called NetChef.

  • Two parts. Enterprise Manager is used at the corporate offices. It holds the company's setup: every product, recipe, vendor and store. NetChef is used in the restaurant: vendor orders, inventories, sales forecasts, the schedule.
  • NetChef talks to the register. It pulls sales, checks and time punches from the POS, which is the register system.
  • What it gives you: orders placed and received in one place, so mistakes are easy to spot. A dashboard of your KPIs (key performance indicators, the few numbers that show how the store is doing). What food cost was, what it should have been, and where to look. Reports to compare weeks. A sales forecast for the week ahead. A task list of what's due.
  • Your part: enter inventories, orders and deliveries accurately, consistently and on time. Everything it tells you is only as good as what goes in.
  • Keep the CrunchTime reference sheet handy. It walks you through each task.

The CrunchTime video says its users routinely lower food cost by 2 to 5% of sales. In a store that does $1 million a year, that's $20,000 to $50,000.

Ordering: the goal and the order guide

Order enough to never run out, and no more than that. The target is enough in the store to last one full business day past your next delivery.

  • Who you order from: Sysco, Pepsi, and in some areas a local produce supplier.
  • Print the order guide from CrunchTime and put it on a clipboard. Walk the store with it.
  • Down the left side, products are grouped by category: all the breads under Food, Bread. All the cheeses under Food, Cheese. Read each product name carefully.
  • Vendor unit is how the product is packed. Red wine vinegar says 4/1 gal: 4 one-gallon bottles in a case. You count and write everything in vendor units.
  • The slash columns are where you work out the order. The next card shows how.
  • Your printed guide may also show par levels (the least and the most to keep on hand), the quantity available, and a 4-week average.

Before you decide

  • Are sales trending up or down? Weather, catering orders, holidays, the season and local events all change how much you need.
  • Do it at the same time each week. It becomes a habit, and stock levels stay steady.
  • Give it time. No distractions. Double-check your work.
  • Don't be the only one who can order. Hand it to someone on the team, then review their order with them.

The slash box math

Each product gets a box split by a slash. Top half: what you have. Bottom half: what you're ordering. Both are in cases, written as decimals.

  1. Write the date at the top of the slash column, on every page.
  2. Count what's on the shelf and turn it into cases. A case of vinegar is 4 bottles, so 2 bottles is 0.5. Write it in the top half.
  3. Decide the order and write it in the bottom half. Half a case won't last, so you order 1.
  4. Next order, count again. 1 bottle left is 0.25.
  5. Work out what you used. You had 0.5 and ordered 1, so 1.5 was in the store. 1.5 minus 0.25 left means 1.25 cases used.
  6. Order with a cushion. One case would bring you to 1.25, exactly what you used. A busy week or a broken bottle and you're out. So you order 2.

Comparing each order with the one before is what makes your ordering precise.

Placing and receiving an order

Placing an order is a short string of clicks. Receiving it means matching the paper invoice to the screen until "over/short" reads 0.

Print the order guide

  1. Quick Links: Create Vendor Order.
  2. Choose the vendor. Put in the expected delivery date. Continue.
  3. Order Guide, top right. Then Export, and print it.

Place the order

  1. Create Vendor Order. Vendor, expected delivery date, Continue.
  2. Type the quantity for each product, from your filled-in guide.
  3. Add Selected Products, top right.
  4. Review the list. Something missing? Retrieve, search for it, add its quantity, and Add Selected Products again.
  5. Prepare Order. Check it one more time. Submit.

Receive it (reconcile)

  • Sysco reconciles on its own most of the time. Pepsi and produce you do by hand.
  • Open Vendor Order Receive. From the paper invoice, type the invoice number and the invoice total, then the actual delivery date and the invoice date. Continue.
  • On the reconcile screen, make it full size with the icon at the top right. Check the two dates again.
  • Match the quantities to the paper invoice. Match the prices to the paper invoice.
  • If everything matches, over/short reads 0. Click Reconcile.
