Tap the clicks in order.

Inventory The weekly count and the math behind it.

Inventory: the math

Inventory answers one question: how much money is all the product in the store worth? From that you get what you used, and food cost.

  • Beginning inventory is the dollar value of the food and paper in the store when the period starts.
  • Purchases are everything delivered during the period: Sysco, Pepsi, produce.
  • Beginning + purchases = working inventory. Everything that was in the store at some point.
  • Closing inventory is the count at the end. It becomes next period's beginning.
  • Working minus closing = cost of goods used. It's shortened to COGU. COGS, cost of goods sold, means the same thing.
  • Divide by sales to get a percent. A percent can be compared with last week and with the store's goal.

The video's example

$5,000 to start + $7,000 in purchases = $12,000. Minus $5,500 at the close = $6,500 used. On sales of $23,215 that's 28%.

When

  • Weekly is best. The period runs Monday through Sunday. A food cost problem gets caught and fixed in days, not weeks.
  • Monthly counts fall on the last Sunday of the month or the last day of the month, depending on how the books are kept.

Put the math in order

Tap the pieces in order.

Before you count

A good count is set up before it starts: an organized store, the right hour, a partner, and the right tools.

  • When: Sunday at close, or Monday before open. The same time every week, and when you're fresh. Not after a long day.
  • Allow at least 1 hour to count. Then separate time to enter it, and time to review it.
  • Sunday evening: stock the working areas early (meat case, sandwich unit, displays). Count the storage areas through the evening. Count the working areas after the store closes.
  • Monday morning: working areas first, then storage. Finish before the store opens. If you can't, storage can still be counted after open.
  • Team up. One counts and weighs, one writes. Then switch. It's the best way to teach someone inventory.
  • Keep the store organized all week. Every delivery goes in its proper place. The count is faster and more accurate.

Bring

  • The count sheet, printed from CrunchTime, on a clipboard.
  • A pencil with an eraser.
  • Extra paper and a calculator.
  • A scale that works and reads right.

The count sheet

One row for each product, grouped by where it's stored. You write how much you have, in whichever unit fits what's in front of you.

  • Seq means sequence. The video leaves the details for a later CrunchTime lesson.
  • Inventory unit is how the item is counted. Bacon is counted by the pound. Other items go by the case, box, sleeve, each, bag or gallon.
  • Qty is where you write how much you have.
  • Alt units are other ways to count the same item. For bacon: case, sheet and slice. So an open case can be 5 pounds, plus 4 full cases, 6 sheets and 12 slices. You count what's there. You don't have to estimate.
  • CrunchTime does the dollars. It multiplies your counts by the current price.
  • Some things do need an estimate, like an open bag-in-the-box of soda. Use sound reasoning.
  • The sheet goes by storage location. Provolone is in the meat case, the walk-in and the sandwich unit. Count everything in one place, then move to the next. No running back and forth.
  • Double-check, above all the decimal points. 0.4 and 4 are very different. A slip like that throws off the whole food cost.

The most common causes of inventory mistakes are carelessness and not paying attention to detail.

Inventory in CrunchTime

Check the invoices, print the sheet, count, type it in, review, post. Then pull the report.

1. Check the purchase journal

  • Purchasing, then Reports, then Purchase Journal. Set the week's dates. Group by supplier. Retrieve.
  • Compare it with your paper invoices. The dates should match, and each order should show a reconciled date.
  • No reconciled date means it hasn't been reconciled. Do that first.
  • An invoice not on the list is usually Pepsi or produce. Place and reconcile it.

2. Print the count sheet

  • Create / Review Inventories. Check the post date. Count Sheet.
  • Filter icon, User-Defined Category. All is all food and paper. Consolidated is breads, meats and cheeses. Weekly Count is all the food and a few paper items. Pick Weekly Count. Apply.
  • Printer icon, Export, print.

3. Count, then enter

  • Create / Review Inventory, post date, Data Entry. Filter to Weekly Count again.
  • Type each count under its proper inventory unit.
  • If any products were left blank, By Exception fills them with an ideal amount, figured from what you started with, ordered and sold.
  • Save and Review. Check the physical column. Wrong number? Edit, fix it, Save and Review again.
  • Save and Close.

4. Post it, then read it

  • Administration, Post Inventory. The summary shows the period's purchases, what was consumed and the ending inventory. If it looks right, Post.
  • Inventory, Reports, Actual Theoretical Cost. Set the dates. Retrieve. Open a category, like meats, to see each product's variance.

Put it in order

Tap the steps in order.

Food cost The goal, the variances, and where to look.

Your food cost goal

CrunchTime tells you what food cost should have been. Add 2 points. That's your goal. Then see how close the real number came.

  • Actual food cost is what it was for the period.
  • Theoretical is what it should have been.
  • Goal = theoretical + 2 points. The 2 points allow for necessary waste and other acceptable things, and make sure guests get enough meat and cheese.
  • The video's example: theoretical 25.71%, so the goal is 27.71%. Actual came in at 28.08%. That's 0.37 over. Food cost is high.
  • The goal belongs to that report only. Next period has a new theoretical and a new goal.
  • Low is as dangerous as high. A number under goal can mean guests are being shorted.

Red and black: reading variances

A variance is the gap between what was used and what should have been used. Red means too much went out. Black means too little did.

  • Red, a negative variance: too much of the product is being used. Example: turkey 78 lb in the red for a week. A turkey weighs about 10.5 lb. That's a whole turkey a day over-portioned or wasted.
  • Black, a positive variance: not enough is being used. Example: provolone 7 lb in the black. Subs went out with too little cheese.
  • Black is just as dangerous as red. It usually means guests aren't getting what they paid for.
  • Some loss is normal. You can't use every last bit of a turkey. 78 lb is far past normal.

First, is the report right?

  1. Is it explainable? A roast beef got burned and thrown out. Product was loaned to another store and never entered. These affect one period only.
  2. Did someone type a number wrong? 1 provolone where it should be 10.
  3. Are all the invoices in and reconciled? Dates, amounts, adjustments. Check the purchase journal.

If it's none of those, the report is accurate, and the answer is in operations: how the store is being run.

Where to look

Two thirds of food cost is meat, cheese and bread. Start there. Work on 3 to 5 variances a week, then check them again the next week.

GroupShare of cost of goods
Meat, cheese, bread67%
Chips, bottled drinks, cookies (all pre-portioned)12%
Other food, and produce20%
Fountain drinks1%

The questions to ask on the floor

  • Are subs sliced correctly? Check slice thickness and the weight of the whole sub.
  • Are ends being sliced down? Meat and cheese ends pile up fast and get expensive.
  • Are recipes followed? Overcooked roast beef or bacon costs you. So does tuna made wrong.
  • Is everything rung up right? A #2 rung in for a #5, or a #7 for an #8, throws off the numbers. Discounts get rung in too. A free dozen cookies for a loyal catering customer is fine. Ring it up.
  • Is the Production Pro chart used every day? Too much bread or bacon made is waste.
  • Bread and meat both negative, week after week? That can mean improper cash handling or theft.
  • Is the team eating the stock? A cookie, a bag of chips, a soda, a strip of bacon. It adds up. They do what they see you do.
  • Are deliveries checked in properly? Damaged or missing product that isn't recorded drives cost up.

The training's line for this: pennies add up to dollars.

The food cost fitness form

When food cost is off and you don't know why, this form lists every cause it could be, each with a page of fixes.

  • The causes it covers: over-portioning and inventory controls. Excessive waste. Poor purchasing and receiving. Product theft. Improper cash handling. Incorrect pricing. Product mix.
  • Not sure which one? Assume you may have all of them.
  • Start with the one you know or suspect. Turn to its solution page and follow it.
  • Do what it takes to prevent every one of them, even the ones that look basic.
  • Still stuck? Ask another store manager, the franchisee or the area director.

Food cost is the biggest expense of running the store. Keeping it on goal is one of a manager's core jobs.

Scheduling and labor Forecast, coverage, labor percent.

Forecast the week's sales

Every schedule starts with one number: what you expect to sell. Labor is the store's second highest cost, and it should never be a surprise.

Two ways to get the number

  • The 4-week average. Add the last 4 weeks of sales. Divide by 4. In the video that comes to $17,535.
  • Last year plus growth. Take the same week last year and add the percent sales are up. Your franchisee has that percent. $16,659.07 plus 5% ($832.95) is $17,492.02.
  • Both land close together. That's a good sign the forecast is reasonable.

Then adjust for what you know

  • Time of year: seasons, holidays, students arriving or leaving.
  • Weather: look at the 10-day forecast. It will change, but it beats going in blind.
  • Community events: a high school football game, a fair, a charity function.
  • Large catering orders that are out of the ordinary.

CrunchTime can forecast for you. The training wants you to know the math behind it anyway. It calls this "knowing the long division."

The coverage chart

For each hour of each day, decide how many fully trained people the store needs. Draw one line for each person's shift.

  1. Get each day's sales. Average the last 4 Mondays for Monday, and so on. The example Monday is $2,249.37, rounded to $2,250.
  2. Draw the opener's line. In the example the manager works 8 to 4. Write the hours: 8.
  3. Add the second person. A shift leader, 9:15 to 1:30. That's 4.25 hours.
  4. Add people as business picks up. A team member 10:30 to 2:30. Another 11:30 to 2. The assistant manager 11:45 to 7:30.
  5. Check the lunch peak. 11:45 to 1:30 has 5 people on.
  6. Draw dinner and close. A shift leader 4 to 9:15. One more person 6 to 9:15. That gives 3 for the dinner peak and 2 to finish closing.
  7. Check the quiet hours too. Enough people to serve guests and finish checklists?

Two rules that never bend

  • At least 2 people in the store during business hours and through closing. The store never closes with fewer than 2.
  • A manager, assistant manager or shift leader is in the store at all times.

The hours and times are the video's example. Every store's busy hours are different, and that's what the chart is for.

Labor percent

Add up what the day's shifts cost. Divide by the day's forecasted sales. That's the labor percent, and you know it before the day happens.

  1. For each person: hours times wage = their pay for the day.
  2. Add everyone's pay. The example Monday comes to $335.75.
  3. Divide by the day's forecasted sales, $2,250. You get 0.1492.
  4. Move the decimal two places right: 14.92%.
  • For the week: add all seven days of pay, then divide by the week's forecasted sales.
  • The goal changes day to day, because sales and coverage do.
  • Looks high or low? Go back to the lines you drew.
  • Try the quarter hour. Start at 10:15 in place of 10:00. End at 2:15 in place of 2:30. Fifteen minutes here and there is a big saving over time.
  • Fully trained people lower labor cost.
  • You don't redraw the chart every week. Do it until you know your store's coverage, and again before any change.

Schedule habits, and the look back

Write it the same time each week, check it before you post it, and after the week ends, ask what it taught you.

Writing it

  • Same time every week. The checklist suggests Thursday afternoon, which leaves time to review and post.
  • Put the shifts into CrunchTime. It shows the forecast and the daily and weekly labor percent.
  • Double-check before posting.
  • Managers work the peaks. That's where a manager can grow sales.
  • Stagger the manager, assistant manager and shift leaders, so strong leadership is always in the store.
  • Enough people for safety.
  • Breaks that follow your local labor laws. That protects everyone.

Ask for each day

  • When do the opener and the second person arrive?
  • When does it pick up enough to need a third?
  • When do the lunch and dinner rushes begin and end?
  • How many are needed in the afternoon to serve guests and finish checklists?
  • Do you need more than 3 for the dinner rush?
  • When do the closers usually finish?

After the week

  • Was the sales forecast accurate?
  • Were there a lot of changes after it was posted?
  • Did weather change it?
  • Did something happen that could have been planned for?
  • What did you learn that you can use next week?

Scheduling is as much about people as it is about money: an honest look at your team's talent, balanced against the store's goals, so the guest always gets great service.

Guests and marketing Four walls, rewards, grassroots.

Four walls marketing

Everything a guest sees, touches and hears inside the store is marketing. A commercial gets 30 seconds. You get at least 3 minutes.

  • An impression is the feeling someone forms without even thinking about it. You get one chance at a first one.
  • The front door: is the glass clean? Is the handle clean?
  • The slicer: guests don't touch it, but they watch it. Keep it clean through the whole rush.
  • Tables: not sticky, and checked often.
  • Napkin dispensers: never dirty.
  • Bathrooms: the cleaner they are, the cleaner guests think the whole store is.
  • Displays: the cookie display, soda case and chip racks full and looking great at all times. That's what prompts the extra purchase.
  • You set the tone: a warm smile, a real greeting, some energy.

What should the logo mean to a guest? In the training's words, the experience and the people first, and then the sandwich.

The tools: points, texts, email, coupons, giving

Five things the store already has for bringing guests back. The strongest one is free: a smile.

  • Shore Points. Ask every guest. The simple way to explain it: buy 12 subs, get the 13th free. Twelve minis earn a mini, twelve regulars a regular, twelve giants a giant. Make sure members get their points every visit.
  • Text messages. A guest joins by text, and that signs them up for Shore Points too. Double points days are announced by text. The company sends one a month. The store manager or franchisee can send up to 3 more.
  • The email club. A sign-up sheet in the store. Monthly offers, and a free sub on the guest's birthday. When a birthday sub comes in, make a big deal of it.
  • Bounce back coupons. A stack of free chip and drink cards and $1 off cards at the register, handed out as a surprise. They bring people back.
  • Giving. "We give to give." March is the Month of Giving. On the Day of Giving, 100% of sales goes to local charities. Fundraising ties the store to its community.

Offers and sign-up details change. The video says about half of all transactions already belong to a member. Check what your store is running now.

A marketing program in 5 steps

Two goals: bring in people who've never tried you, and bring current guests in more often. Five steps, and then you do them again.

  1. Plan. Who goes out, and where. It should be someone who can be themselves away from the counter. A marketing map hangs in the back room. Know everything within 1 mile: every street, business and school.
  2. Prepare. Menus, flyers, free sub cards. Ordered and in stock before you go.
  3. Implement. Run a program from the local store marketing manual. Some happen inside the store, some outside it.
  4. Evaluate. After each visit, write notes on their business card: which free sub cards you left (say, 11 through 17), how many employees, do they hold meetings, do they cater. Log it on the tracking sheet. Did the cards come back? If not, why?
  5. Re-implement. Marketing is never one time. In retail, staff turn over about every 3 months, so the people you met are probably gone.
  • Ways to split the map: pie slices, puzzle pieces, or by kind of business (churches and schools, small businesses, large retailers).
  • Cards that never come back tell you something. Maybe that business can't get out for lunch, and online ordering or delivery would fit them.

Put the steps in order

Tap the steps in order.

Grassroots

Grassroots is walking into the businesses near your store, saying who you are, and inviting people in for lunch. You aren't selling anything.

  • New guests: buy them lunch. A free sub card gets the first try.
  • Current guests: give them options. If they can't get out, show them online ordering or delivery.
  • Catering is not grassroots. It follows by itself once people have tried the food.

Ground rules

  • Set a reasonable goal. Two hours out might be a couple hundred cards, each with a real conversation. Not a thousand cards dropped.
  • Relax and be yourself. You're meeting neighbors.
  • Be patient. They have customers and phones. You come second.
  • Smile, make eye contact.
  • Be able to say exactly where your store is.
  • Nervous is okay. It gets easier every time.

Planning it

  • Go when the store can spare you. After the opening is done and the second person is in. About 9 to 10:30 or 11.
  • Not on a truck day.
  • Trust the team. If you can't leave and stop checking your phone, it's not the day.
  • Bring: menus, free sub cards, and a way to show online ordering or delivery.
  • Keep it simple. A few offers, not fifteen. Fewer are easier to track.
  • Carry free sub cards every time you leave the store. The bank, the gas station, the gym. Invite someone in every day.

The visit: big stores, small shops, offices

Each kind of business has a best time to visit and one person worth knowing.

Big-box stores
When: early, right after they open. Who: the manager. You'll only reach one or two people, but the manager can bring you into a morning meeting or pass cards to the staff. Get a name, a number and a business card.
Small shops
When: any time of day. Who: the owner or manager, and then every employee. With a small staff you can invite each one in person.
Offices
When: it depends. A doctor's office first thing, before patients. A big office building any time. Who: the receptionist, who usually orders lunch. Be patient and kind. Dress the part: for office buildings, a pressed Oxford shirt.

What to say

  1. Your name, and that you're from the store down the street.
  2. "Have you ever been in?"
  3. If no: ask how many work there and if they can get out for lunch. Hand them a free sub card. No catches. "I'd love to make you lunch."
  4. If yes: thank them. Give them a card for their next visit. Ask to meet the rest of the staff.
  5. Ask for their business card before you go.

Catering comes up only when it fits. In the training's role play the manager already loved the food and mentioned monthly staff meetings, so offering a tray made sense.

Profit and the P&L The four keys, bread math, the monthly report.

Run it like you own it

Profit is what happens when everything is done right. Act like the owner before you are one, and people notice.

  • Want a raise? Work as though you already have it.
  • Want to be the manager? Show a manager's habits now.
  • Want your own store someday? Take pride in every sub and every guest.

What that looks like

  • Look people in the eyes.
  • Speak with confidence, and with humility.
  • Make every sub with enough meat and enough juice, with urgency.
  • Seek out people who have done it before, and listen.
  • Make the people around you happy. Be the one everyone wants to work with, not the dark cloud.
  • Be responsible with your own money.
  • Be on the front line with your team. Lead by doing.
  • Be patient and humble. Doors open.

The four keys

Four numbers decide profit: sales, food cost, labor cost, and what's left. Take care of the first three and the fourth follows.

1. Top line sales
The store's total sales. Grow them by valuing every guest: the right amount of meat and cheese, enough juice, and a reason to come back. Four walls marketing and grassroots feed this.
2. Food cost
Order well, count weekly, read what CrunchTime tells you, and use the food cost fitness form when it's off.
3. Labor cost
Know the flow of your business, so people are there when guests are. Invest in training: a trained team lowers labor and usually helps sales and food cost too. Change the plan mid-shift when the day calls for it.
4. The bottom line
What's left. Protect it by watching the other three.

Bread math

Bread is on every sub, so it measures the whole business. Two numbers: sales per loaf, and loaves per day.

  • Average sales per loaf = the week's sales divided by the week's loaves. $16,500 on 1,000 loaves is $16.50. Size and add-ons are already inside that number.
  • Average bread per day = the week's loaves divided by 7. 1,000 loaves is 143 a day.
  • The goal: 10 more loaves a day. At $16.50 that's $165 a day, or $1,155 a week. The week goes from $16,500 to $17,655.

Raising sales per loaf

  • Offer the add-ons: chips and a drink, a fresh baked cookie. Ask without sounding like a recording.
  • Ring up the extras: extra meat, extra cheese, bacon.
  • Minis and regulars: three minis bring in more than one giant. So do two regulars.
  • Pricing: the home office sets recommended prices.

The P&L, top half

The P&L is a monthly report card for the store's money. Sales at the top, what's left at the bottom, and every cost in between.

Sales

  • Gross sales: the value of everything the team made, before discounts and coupons.
  • Net sales: the money that actually came in.
  • The gap is your discounts and coupons. Watch it month to month, above all after a promotion. Example: $94,587 gross, $89,976 net.

Cost of goods

  • Food is the biggest number, and one you control every day. It should sit about 2 points above CrunchTime's theoretical. Example: 26.1%.
  • Paper usually runs 1.5 to 2%. Nearer 2.5% usually means a lot of catering: boxes, bags, supplies. Example: 1.9%.

Facility: mostly fixed

  • Rent: the aim is 8% of sales or less. It includes CAM (common area maintenance: landscaping, snow removal, the roof), taxes and insurance. Example: 4.2%.
  • Repairs and maintenance: kept in line by following the preventative maintenance schedule.
  • Computer: fees for the register software, CrunchTime, the online ordering app.
  • Utilities: usually 1.5 to 2.5%. Watch for jumps. A water bill that shoots up may be a leaky toilet.
  • Waste removal and insurance.
  • You can't change these day to day, but habits help: equipment kept up, the bread oven off when it isn't in use. Example total: 7%.

The P&L, bottom half

Labor is the second biggest cost and the other one you control. Below it sit supplies and fees. What's left is called EBITDA.

Labor

  • Hourly labor: usually 12 to 16% of sales. This one line is what people mean by "the labor number."
  • Hourly plus management: usually 20 to 22%. The two are kept on separate lines so problems are easy to see.
  • Payroll taxes rise and fall with payroll dollars.
  • Workers' compensation comes down when training and safety prevent injuries.
  • Example, everything in: 22.5%.

Operations

  • Over and short: the cash that should be in the drawer against what was deposited. With good cash handling it barely moves. The example is $1.81 short for the month.
  • Supplies: linens (towels, aprons, floor mats), office supplies, gloves (about a quarter to half a percent of sales), cleaning supplies, small kitchen tools.
  • The rest: delivery and catering service fees, local advertising, accounting, training, licenses, uniforms, donations.
  • Theft has its own line: cash that went missing between the drawer and the deposit.

Fees to the brand

The royalty. Corporate advertising, which is what you see inside the store. The national media fee: TV, radio, billboards.

EBITDA

  • It stands for earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. In plain words: what the store earned from running, before loans and taxes.
  • The store's P&L stops there on purpose. It shows only what the people in the store can affect. Example: 25.8%.
  • A healthy P&L: grow sales, keep food within 2 points of theoretical, forecast labor and adjust during the week. Teach your team the parts they affect.

Put the P&L in order

Tap the sections from the top of the page down.

The weekly review

One sheet, once a week: find about a dozen numbers, write them side by side with the weeks before, and circle the ones to fix.

From the register's reports, for last Monday through Sunday

  • Sales, ticket count, average check.
  • Bread, average bread per day (bread divided by 7), average sales per loaf.
  • Discounts and coupons.
  • Voids, refunds, cancelled tickets.
  • Shore Points members.

From CrunchTime

  • Actual food cost, theoretical food cost, and the variance between them. Inventory, Reports, Actual Theoretical Cost.
  • Actual labor percent. Labor, Reports, Daily Payroll Control.

Then

Line the week up next to the weeks before it. The sheet holds up to five. Circle any number that needs work, and improve it during the week you're in.
